questions.q: What is the fundamental physical difference between guided and unguided transmission media that determines how signals propagate?
questions.a: Guided media uses physical conductors (copper wires or glass fibers) that physically confine and direct electromagnetic signals along a specific path, while unguided media transmits signals as electromagnetic waves radiating through air, vacuum, or water without any physical guiding structure. A wrong answer (e.g., "guided is faster" or "guided uses wires, unguided doesn't") reveals the student is confusing performance characteristics with the defining physical mechanism of signal propagation.

questions.q: A student claims: "Optical fiber is always better than twisted pair cable because it has higher bandwidth." Explain why this statement is an oversimplification by identifying three specific scenarios where twisted pair would be the more appropriate choice.
questions.a: Twisted pair is more appropriate when: (1) Cost is critical for short distances (e.g., home/office LANs under 100m) where Cat6 UTP costs ₹15-25/meter vs fiber at ₹50-100/meter plus expensive transceivers; (2) Ease of installation and termination matters - twisted pair uses simple RJ45 connectors crimped with basic tools, while fiber requires fusion splicing or precision polishing; (3) Power over Ethernet (PoE) is needed for devices like IP cameras or VoIP phones - copper carries both data and DC power, fiber cannot. A wrong answer focusing only on bandwidth reveals the student cannot evaluate engineering trade-offs beyond raw specifications.

questions.q: Your school wants to connect two buildings 800 meters apart across a public road where digging permission is denied. The network requires 1 Gbps bandwidth. Compare the feasibility of: (a) Outdoor-rated Cat6 UTP with media converters, (b) Single-mode fiber optic cable on aerial poles, (c) Wireless microwave link. Recommend the best option with justification.
questions.a: (a) Cat6 UTP: Maximum segment length is 100m per TIA/EIA-568 standard; 800m requires 7 repeaters/switches with power sources - impractical across a road. (b) Single-mode fiber: Supports 10+ Gbps at 800m easily, immune to EMI from traffic, aerial installation avoids digging - best technical fit. (c) Microwave link: Requires line-of-sight, licensed spectrum, precise alignment, susceptible to rain fade - overkill for 800m. Recommendation: Single-mode fiber on aerial poles. A wrong answer choosing microwave (thinking "wireless is easier") reveals misunderstanding of microwave's alignment complexity and licensing requirements vs fiber's straightforward aerial deployment.

questions.q: Analyze why coaxial cable, despite having higher bandwidth than twisted pair (up to 10 Gbps for short runs), has been largely replaced by twisted pair in modern LANs and by fiber in backbone networks. Identify the specific electrical and economic factors.
questions.a: Coaxial cable declined due to: (1) Impedance mismatch sensitivity - BNC connectors and T-connectors in bus topologies caused signal reflections; twisted pair's point-to-point star topology with switches eliminates this. (2) Bulk and bend radius - RG-6 coax is 7mm diameter with 35mm minimum bend radius vs Cat6 UTP at 6mm with 25mm bend radius, making coax harder to route in dense cable trays. (3) Cost per port - Coax requires expensive transceivers (AUI/10BASE2) while twisted pair uses ubiquitous, cheap RJ45 ports on commodity switches. (4) No PoE capability - Coax cannot carry DC power for devices. Fiber replaced coax in backbones due to vastly superior distance (km vs 500m) and bandwidth (Tbps vs Gbps). A wrong answer citing only "coax is old" reveals inability to analyze specific electrical engineering and economic drivers of technology adoption.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "For a rural school in hilly terrain needing internet connectivity, satellite link is the best transmission medium." Consider latency, bandwidth asymmetry, weather dependence, cost, and alternatives like long-range Wi-Fi or TV white space.
questions.a: The claim is generally FALSE for interactive educational use. Geostationary satellite (35,786 km altitude) imposes ~550ms round-trip latency, making video conferencing, VoIP, and real-time collaboration unusable. Bandwidth is typically asymmetric (high downlink, low uplink ~1-3 Mbps), problematic for uploading assignments. Rain fade in monsoon disrupts Ku-band signals. Cost: ₹5000-15000/month for 10-50 Mbps vs long-range Wi-Fi (5-15 km with directional antennas, ₹50,000 one-time, 100+ Mbps, <5ms latency) or TV white space (unused TV channels, 10+ km, penetrates foliage). Satellite is only justified when NO terrestrial or wireless backhaul exists. A wrong answer accepting the claim reveals inability to quantify latency impact on TCP throughput and user experience, and ignorance of emerging rural connectivity alternatives.

questions.q: Design a transmission media plan for a new 3-story school building with: 40 classrooms (25 computers each), 5 labs (40 computers each), admin block (30 computers), and a server room in the basement. Specify media type for each segment (horizontal cabling, backbone, inter-building if campus expands), justify each choice with distance, bandwidth, and cost reasoning, and draw a simple topology diagram description.
questions.a: A strong answer specifies: Horizontal (workstation to floor switch): Cat6a UTP (10 Gbps at 100m, ₹25/m, PoE+ for APs/cameras) - 125 runs × 3 floors = 375 drops. Backbone (floor switches to core in basement): OM4 multimode fiber (100 Gbps at 100m, ₹80/m) - 3 runs, future-proof for 40/100G upgrade. Inter-building (if campus expands): Single-mode fiber (10+ km, 100 Gbps) on aerial/duct. Topology: Star-wired hierarchical - each floor has 2×48-port PoE+ switches (access layer) uplinked via 10G SFP+ to core switch (distribution) in basement. Server room connects to core via 10G/25G DAC or fiber. A poor answer uses same media everywhere, ignores PoE needs, omits backbone vs horizontal distinction, or suggests wireless for stationary desktops.
